title: the Sri Sukta
hook: the hymn wants the goddess of fortune in the house, and the first one it speaks to is the fire

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Sri Sukta began with a portrait: golden, garlanded in gold and silver, shining like the moon. Did you find a light you didn't make, and count it? Day one thousand ninety-one.

There's an old way to meet someone important: don't knock on their door yourself. Ask someone who already knows them, a cousin, a teacher, a friend of a friend. Make the introduction. Bring them by. The Sri Sukta does exactly that. The singer wants Sri, the goddess of fortune, in the house. But the first words of request aren't spoken to her at all. They're spoken to the fire. Yesterday was the portrait at the start of the opening verse. Today, the end of that same verse: a short request, and the one it's said to. Bring her to me, fire.
screen: `ASK SOMEONE WHO KNOWS THEM.` → `THE FIRST REQUEST ISN'T TO HER.` → `BRING HER TO ME, FIRE.`

segments.voice: The verse ends, in paraphrase: O Jatavedas, bring Lakshmi to me. Jatavedas is a name of Agni, the fire. Start with what the fire does in the Vedas. In the opening hymn of the Rig Veda, Agni is praised as the priest of the sacrifice, the one who will bring the gods here. Offerings go into the fire, and the fire brings the gods. Fire is the go-between. So when the Sri Sukta asks the fire to bring Lakshmi, it's asking the fire to do its old work. Second, the little word for bring: avaha, bring here, carry this way. It isn't go and get. It's closer to a host saying to a friend: please bring her by. The singer stays home and keeps the fire going, and trusts the fire to make the introduction. Third, what's quietly assumed. You can't ask a fire for anything if there isn't one burning. A household fire has to be tended: fuel, care, someone to watch it. The request depends on that steady small work. Some readers hear a plain lesson in it: fortune is asked for through something you already keep alive at home. Fourth, the lamp. In some Hindu homes, small lamps are lit when Lakshmi is welcomed, especially at Diwali, along windowsills and doorsteps. The fire is still the go-between, now small enough to sit in a clay cup. Whether the fire is a great altar or one wick in oil, the shape of the request is the same: a light is kept burning, and the goddess is asked to come by it.
screen: `JATAVEDAS: A NAME OF AGNI, THE FIRE.` · `FIRE IS THE GO-BETWEEN.` · `AVAHA: PLEASE BRING HER BY.` · `A FIRE THAT SOMEONE KEEPS.` · then, large: `BRING LAKSHMI TO ME.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: feed the fire. Sit, and let the breath settle. Picture a small household fire, low and steady. With each in-breath, picture laying one small stick on it. With each out-breath, watch it settle and glow. Not too much, or it smokes; not too little, or it fades. Just one stick a breath, keeping it alive. Let the breath find that same even pace. If you pray, you can ask the fire, as the hymn does, to bring good fortune to your house, or speak to God in the words you use. If you don't, let the flame stand for whatever you hope will come. The bell holds the time.
The Sri Sukta. In its opening verse, the singer asks Jatavedas, the fire, to bring Lakshmi: the fire as the go-between.
Your line: the Sri Sukta. Today, tend one small thing that keeps your home alive: water a plant, cook one meal, fix one light. Day one thousand ninety-one.

howItsDone: In Lakshmi worship and Vedic rites, the Sri Sukta is chanted before a lamp or sacred fire, and some households light small lamps at Diwali to welcome the goddess.

fork.setup: you're the singer. you want Sri, the goddess of fortune, to come to your house. who do you ask first?
options: the fire, Jatavedas: bring her to me.
nobody: you wait for her to arrive.
fork.reveal: the opening verse ends: O Jatavedas, bring Lakshmi to me. the fire is the go-between, as Agni is in the Vedas.

original.note: Sanskrit: Jatavedas, a name of Agni, the fire, asked to bring Lakshmi in the Sri Sukta.

trapdoor: what you thought: the hymn speaks only to the goddess.
what it means: its first request goes to the fire, the old go-between, asked to bring her to the house.
what a scholar hears: jātavedo ma āvaha, O Jatavedas, bring to me, echoing Rig Veda 1.1.2, sa devāṁ eha vakṣati: he shall bring the gods here.
recall: a warrior, and a daughter coming home
the year just walked and kept

notes: Sri Sukta 1 paraphrased (jātavedo ma āvaha). Day 1092 (another writer) also explains Jatavedas briefly as the fire who carries offerings; an editor may trim one of the two.
Rig Veda 1.1.1–2 paraphrased: Agni as purohita / hotar of the sacrifice, and 'sa devāṁ eha vakṣati', he shall bring the gods here. The trapdoor's 'echoing' is an interpretive link; Keeper to confirm.
Jatavedas glossed only as 'a name of Agni'; the usual 'knower of all born beings' gloss was left out under the etymology rule.
'avaha: bring here, carry this way' is a gloss of meaning (ā + vah); confirm.
Diwali lamps described with 'some households'; Keeper to confirm.

Editor pass: hook's garbled 'the newcomer asks someone who knows them' rewritten; 'two small words' (the Sanskrit is three, jātavedo ma āvaha) became 'a short request'; the offerings-rise/gods-come-down 'road' image, not in Rig Veda 1.1, trimmed in teach and myth; 'someone up early' changed to avoid echoing day 1092; practice changed from gazing at a candle (repeated day 1081's flame practice) to feeding an imagined fire with the breath.
